newsitem.title: UK: EMS REPORT - EMS/Mark softer on crosses, Nordics outperform.
newsitem.headline: EMS REPORT - EMS/Mark softer on crosses, Nordics outperform.

text.p: The German mark was softer on its European cross rates early Wednesday, weighed down by a rampaging dollar, news of another rise in German unemployment in July and an unexpectedly generous addition of liquidity at the Bundesbank's weekly money market operation.
The dollar surged to near eight year highs of 1.89 marks, while sterling suffered against both the dollar and mark on last minute jitters about the chances for a UK rate rise this week.
German government spokesman Peter Hausmann said later that the dollar move was speculative and Bonn saw no need to change its existing currency policy.

"The German jobless numbers were very disappointing again and with the labour market there remaining so stagnant, it leaves the Bundesbank very little room to manoeuvre," said Brian Martin, chief economist, FX at BZW.
The German unemployment rate rose to a seasonally-adjusted 11.5 percent from 11.4 percent in June and 10.3 in July of last year. The adjusted total jobless rose 17,000 during the month.

Earlier, the Bundesbank added a net 2.6 billion marks of new funds to the local money markets at its regular securities repurchase tender, a move which did little to fuel speculation of an imminent rise in its 3.0 percent repo rate.

"Further increases in unemployment and falls in personal sector spending only serve to highlight the Bundesbank's dilemma," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. "Although a weak mark - and its effect on import prices - is an obvious concern, it is equally clear that a rise in interest rates is the last thing the economy needs."

A Bundesbank spokesman denied rumours late Tuesday that the central bank's policy-making council, currently on its summer recess, was due to convene this week for an emergency meeting. The bank's Frankfurt-based directorate, however, talk regularly and were likely to be in regular contact, analysts said.

There has been a wave of speculation in recent weeks that the weakness of the mark, particularly against the dollar, would force the Bundesbank to allow its key money market interest rate to tick higher to shore up the currency.

As optimism about a punctual start to European monetary union remains high, the likely EMU currencies continue to trade more or less like a bloc and this is limiting turbulence on most of the mark's European cross rates.
At 1030 GMT, mark/French franc was at 3.3753/58 compared with 3.3759/61 late Tuesday. Mark/lira was at 978.65/75 versus 978.90/20 late yesterday.
With sterling bulls suffering from a bout of insecurity, the Nordic currencies outperformed against the softer mark as investors search for other non-EMU floating currencies.
Mark/Swedish crown was at 4.2910/40 compared with 4.3010/40 and Mark/Norwegian was at 4.1075/05 compared with 4.1230/60.
Elsewhere, the economic news was not as bleak as in Germany.

Spanish unemployment fell to its lowest level in 16 years at 12.5 percent in July and French industrialists said they see third-quarter manufacturing demand rising at the same rate as the second quarter.
